episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Cariboo Local Affairs
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Cariboo Local Affairs.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Is it better to be self-sufficient or well-connected?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [My Cariboo Now] Millar Western to curtail operations at Quesnel River Pulp at end of day and [Williams Lake Tribune] B.C. sheds 5,500 jobs in August amid nationwide losses, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Does Quesnel need to develop a repeatable, documented process for siting difficult facilities like shelters, or can it continue to handle each proposal case-by-case as political circumstances demand? Topics include: The distinction between self-sufficiency and provincial partnership in rural governance, Whether the BC NIMBY Toolkit prevents reversals or only earlier-stage collapses, The absence of lived-experience voices in facility siting decisions, Institutional knowledge versus fresh perspective in the mayoral/council candidates Leclerc and Cave, The need for written, repeatable criteria matrices that survive across multiple council terms.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Quesnel Shelter & Support Society

discussion.central_question: Does Quesnel need to develop a repeatable, documented process for siting difficult facilities like shelters, or can it continue to handle each proposal case-by-case as political circumstances demand?
discussion.riley_position: Quesnel lacks a standing infrastructure for recurring crises and needs written siting criteria that survive past individual council terms and neighborhood opposition. The real gap is the absence of a systematic, documented process that includes people with lived experience from the start.
riley_key_evidence: BC's NIMBY Toolkit exists specifically because supportive housing hits neighborhood resistance everywhere, and communities that engage neighbors early see fewer reversals
Tammy Janzen pointed out that people who'd actually use the shelter aren't in the room when the site gets chosen
The underlying issue mirrors the Cariboo Regional District's fire-season response pattern: rebuilding approach from nothing every time instead of having standing infrastructure
discussion.casey_position: Quesnel followed a formal process with a public hearing and approved permit in July, yet council still reversed course on the extension, showing that process alone doesn't prevent political reversals when neighborhood pressure builds. The toolkit and provincial best practice didn't stop this outcome.
casey_key_evidence: Council approved a temporary use permit in July but then voted down BC Housing's request for a two-year extension weeks later despite the public process
Even with the NIMBY Toolkit's best practices, the shelter reversal happened anyway on schedule under the funding deadline
Quesnel is now holding both costs: political fallout from its own reversal plus running against BC Housing's timeline with no confirmed alternative site
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey agreed to disagree on whether provincial tools prevent reversals, but converged on the structural solution: Quesnel council should be directly asked whether written siting criteria and a role for lived-experience input actually exist in any documented form, making this question actionable for residents at public meetings without waiting for external programs.
